what_its_for: Osilodrostat is used to treat adults with Cushing's disease — a condition where your body makes too much of a hormone called cortisol. This usually happens because of a tumor on the pituitary gland in your brain. This medicine works by blocking an enzyme in your adrenal glands (located above your kidneys) that helps make cortisol, which lowers your cortisol levels back toward normal.
how_to_take: Take osilodrostat by mouth, twice a day — once in the morning and once in the evening, about 12 hours apart. You can take it with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole. Try to take it at the same times every day to keep steady levels of the medicine in your body. Do not crush, chew, or split the tablets unless your doctor or pharmacist says it is okay.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a low dose (usually 2 mg twice a day) and slowly adjust it based on how your cortisol levels respond and how well you tolerate the medicine. The dose is increased gradually — typically every 2 weeks — until your cortisol is at a normal level. The maximum dose is 30 mg twice a day. Never change your dose on your own. Your doctor will do regular blood and urine tests to check your cortisol levels and make sure the dose is right for you.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still several hours before your next scheduled dose. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and take the next one at your regular time. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store osilodrostat at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it in its original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines safely out of the reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking medicines that can cause an irregular heartbeat (QT prolongation) without first talking to your doctor, as osilodrostat can also affect heart rhythm. Tell your doctor and pharmacist about ALL medicines you take — including prescription, over-the-counter, vitamins, and herbal supplements — because osilodrostat can interact with many medications. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice unless your doctor says it is okay. Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor, as your cortisol levels could drop too low.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you experience: signs of low cortisol (adrenal insufficiency) such as extreme tiredness, weakness, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, or low blood pressure; signs of high male hormones such as acne, unusual hair growth on face or body, or irregular menstrual periods in women; a fast, slow, or irregular heartbeat or chest pain (possible heart rhythm problem); severe skin rash or allergic reaction such as swelling of face, lips, tongue, or throat; signs of liver problems such as yellowing of skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain. Also tell your doctor if you feel unusually tired, have mood changes, or feel faint when standing up.
when_it_works: Osilodrostat starts working fairly quickly — your cortisol levels may begin to drop within the first few days of treatment. However, it may take several weeks to months before your symptoms of Cushing's disease — such as weight gain, easy bruising, stretch marks, muscle weakness, and mood changes — start to get noticeably better. Your doctor will check your cortisol levels regularly to make sure the medicine is working properly and to adjust your dose if needed. Be patient and keep taking the medicine as prescribed.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Osilodrostat may harm an unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant should use effective birth control while taking this medicine and tell their doctor right away if they become pregnant. Breastfeeding: It is not known if this medicine passes into breast milk. Do not breastfeed while taking osilodrostat. Liver problems: If you have moderate to severe liver disease, your doctor may start you on a lower dose and monitor you more closely. Kidney problems: No dose adjustment is usually needed for kidney problems, but your doctor will decide what is best for you. Heart conditions: Tell your doctor if you have a history of heart rhythm problems (such as QT prolongation), low potassium or magnesium levels, or are taking other medicines that affect heart rhythm. Older adults: Use with caution — your doctor will monitor you carefully for side effects.
